name: Covenant Theology
tagline: One covenant of grace, one people of God, from Eden to the new creation.
selfDescription: Covenant (or 'federal') theologians describe Scripture as the unfolding of God's covenants: an eternal covenant of redemption within the Trinity, a covenant of works with Adam, and a single covenant of grace announced in Genesis 3:15 and administered in successive covenants until it is fulfilled in Christ's new covenant. They speak of 'one people of God' and of the church as Israel's fulfilment, 'Israel expanded' to include the Gentiles. Most reject the label “replacement theology,” preferring “fulfillment” or “expansion”: Israel was not replaced but brought to its goal in Christ, the true Israel.
summary: Covenant theology is the classic Reformed framework for reading the Bible as a unified story. It emphasises continuity: one covenant of grace in substance under different administrations (promise, Mosaic, new), one people of God in both Testaments, and Christ as the fulfilment of Israel's promises. On Israel and the church it holds that the church, Jewish and Gentile believers grafted into one olive tree (Romans 11:17-24), is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel, not a parenthesis. Within that consensus covenant theologians differ on whether Romans 11:26 promises a future mass conversion of ethnic Israel (affirmed by many Puritans, Hodge, Vos, John Murray; denied by others who read 'all Israel' as the elect of all ages). Eschatologically, covenant theologians are predominantly amillennial or postmillennial, with a minority of historic premillennialists; dispensational premillennialism is incompatible with the framework.
coreBeliefs: The covenant of redemption (pactum salutis): an eternal agreement in which the Father gives a people to the Son, who undertakes to redeem them, applied by the Spirit (John 6:37-40; 17:4-6; Ephesians 1:3-14).
The covenant of works (or of life/creation) with Adam as federal head of humanity, broken in the fall, whose curse Christ the last Adam bears and whose reward he earns (Hosea 6:7; Romans 5:12-21).
One covenant of grace, first announced in Genesis 3:15, administered through the covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses and David and fulfilled in the new covenant (Westminster Confession 7.5-6).

One people of God throughout redemptive history: believing Israel and the church are one olive tree (Romans 11:17-24), one household (Ephesians 2:11-22), and believers in Christ are Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:7, 29).

On Israel: fulfilment or expansion, not replacement. Christ is the true Israel (Isaiah 49:3; Matthew 2:15), and the promises of land, temple and kingdom find their 'yes' in him (2 Corinthians 1:20) and the new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:10-16).

Many covenant theologians expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews (Romans 11:12, 15, 25-26) into the one church, not a separate national programme; others read 'all Israel' as the full number of elect Jews (or of all the elect).
The law is distinguished as moral, ceremonial and civil (judicial); the moral law continues as a rule of life while the ceremonial is fulfilled in Christ (Westminster Confession 19.3-5).

Continuity of covenant signs: most (Presbyterian, Reformed, Anglican) baptise infants of believers as the new-covenant counterpart to circumcision (Colossians 2:11-12; Acts 2:39), while Baptist covenant theology (1689 Federalism) baptises believers only.

history.text: Irenaeus traced God's dealings through successive covenants and stressed the unity of the Old and New Testaments against Marcion; Augustine's City of God presented one people of God across history and spoke of a covenant with Adam.

Huldrych Zwingli and Heinrich Bullinger (On the One and Eternal Testament or Covenant of God, 1534) argued for the unity of the covenant against Anabaptists. Calvin's Institutes (2.10-11) set out the similarity and difference of the Testaments; Ursinus, Olevianus and Robert Rollock developed the covenant of works.

The Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 7) codified the covenants of works and grace; Johannes Cocceius, Francis Turretin, John Owen (on Hebrews) and Herman Witsius (The Economy of the Covenants, 1677) systematised federal theology. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) framed a Baptist covenant theology.

Charles Hodge and the Princeton theologians, Southern Presbyterians, and the Dutch Reformed (Herman Bavinck) carried the system forward; Geerhardus Vos founded Reformed biblical theology on the covenants. Louis Berkhof's Systematic Theology became a standard text; John Murray reworked the covenant of works, and Meredith Kline developed the role of works in the Mosaic covenant.

Michael Horton, O. Palmer Robertson (The Christ of the Covenants; The Israel of God), Richard Belcher, J. V. Fesko, Kim Riddlebarger, Samuel Waldron and Pascal Denault (1689 Federalism) are leading voices; theonomic postmillennialists (Bahnsen, Gentry) also work within covenant theology.

strengths: Accounts for the deep unity of Scripture and the New Testament's insistence that Gentile believers are children of Abraham and fellow citizens with Israel's saints.
Follows the apostolic pattern of reading Old Testament promises Christologically (Acts 13:32-34; 2 Corinthians 1:20).
Supplies a theology of federal headship that explains both the fall in Adam and justification in Christ (Romans 5).
Has long confessional and historical pedigree across Presbyterian, Reformed, Anglican and Reformed Baptist churches.
Avoids a two-peoples model while still allowing (in many proponents) a future in-grafting of ethnic Israel.

critiques.critique: The covenants of redemption and works are theological constructs: Scripture never names them.
critiques.response: Covenant theologians answer that the elements of a covenant (parties, stipulation, promise, sanction) are present in Genesis 2, that Hosea 6:7 refers to Adam's covenant breaking, and that Paul's Adam-Christ parallel requires federal headship. The Trinity is also an unnamed but necessary synthesis of biblical data.

critiques.critique: It is 'replacement theology' (supersessionism), which nullifies God's irrevocable promises to ethnic Israel (Romans 11:29) and has historically fed contempt for Jews.
critiques.response: Most covenant theologians reject the label. They argue that Israel was not replaced but fulfilled in Christ and expanded to include Gentiles (Ephesians 2:14-16; Romans 11:17-24), so believing Jews remain the natural branches. Many affirm a future mass conversion of Jews (Romans 11:26), and they repudiate anti-Judaism as contrary to Romans 11:18-20.

critiques.critique: It flattens the discontinuity between the Testaments, especially the newness of the new covenant, in which all members know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11).
critiques.response: Covenant theology distinguishes the substance of the covenant of grace (one) from its administrations (many), affirming real progress from shadow to reality (Westminster Confession 7.5-6). Paedobaptists argue that the new covenant still has a visible community including children (Acts 2:39), while Baptist covenant theologians agree that the new covenant community should be regenerate.

critiques.critique: Infant baptism rests on an inference from circumcision rather than explicit New Testament command.
critiques.response: Paedobaptists point to the continuity of the household principle (Genesis 17:7; Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 7:14) and the link between circumcision and baptism (Colossians 2:11-12). Moreover, covenant theology is not identical with paedobaptism: 1689 Federalists hold the same framework with believer's baptism.

subViews.name: Westminster (paedobaptist) covenant theology
subViews.summary: The mainstream Presbyterian and Continental Reformed form: one covenant of grace in substance under the old and new administrations, with children of believers as members of the visible covenant community and baptised accordingly. Representative: Westminster Confession, Witsius, Turretin, Hodge, Berkhof, Robertson, Horton.

subViews.name: 1689 Federalism (Reformed Baptist)
subViews.summary: Baptist covenant theology rooted in the Second London Confession (1689) and writers such as Nehemiah Coxe: the covenant of grace was promised in the Old Testament but formally established only in the new covenant, whose members are all regenerate. The Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants are typological and distinct from the covenant of grace itself. Representative: Pascal Denault, Samuel Waldron.

subViews.name: Klinean / republication emphasis
subViews.summary: Following Meredith Kline, some (e.g. Michael Horton, many at Westminster Seminary California) hold that the Mosaic covenant republished a works principle at a typological level, governing Israel's tenure in the land, while salvation was always by grace. This strand often pairs with amillennialism and a sharp distinction between common and holy realms. Others (e.g. John Murray's tradition) contest republication.

subViews.name: Covenantal views of 'all Israel' (Romans 11:26)
subViews.summary: Covenant theologians divide over Romans 11:26. One view, common among Puritans and Princeton theologians and held by Vos, John Murray, and many postmillennialists and some amillennialists, expects a future mass conversion of ethnic Jews, incorporated into the one church. A second sees 'all Israel' as the total number of elect Jews saved throughout history (Hoekema, Robertson). A third (Calvin's reading, also N. T. Wright) takes 'all Israel' as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile.

name: Dispensationalism
tagline: God's distinct programmes for Israel and the church, read with a consistent literal hermeneutic.
selfDescription: Dispensationalists describe their system as the result of 'consistent literal' (normal, grammatical-historical) interpretation applied across Scripture, including prophecy. Charles Ryrie named three marks, his 'sine qua non': a consistent literal hermeneutic, a distinction between Israel and the church, and the glory of God (not only redemption) as history's unifying purpose. Today many prefer to describe their view of Israel as 'non-supersessionist', affirming the ongoing theological significance of ethnic, national Israel.
summary: Dispensationalism is a framework for reading Scripture that sees history as a series of dispensations, distinct stewardships in which God tests humanity under different arrangements, and, above all, maintains a distinction between Israel and the church. God's unconditional covenants with Abraham, David and Israel (the land, throne and new covenant) will be fulfilled literally to national Israel, chiefly in a future millennial kingdom; the church, born at Pentecost, is a distinct body of Jews and Gentiles in Christ. Eschatologically it is always premillennial (dispensational premillennialism) and usually pretribulational. It developed through classic (Darby, Scofield, Chafer), revised (Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost) and progressive (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) phases.
coreBeliefs: A consistent literal (normal, grammatical-historical) hermeneutic, including for prophetic texts; New Testament use of the Old does not cancel the original meaning of promises to Israel.
Israel and the church are distinct: the church is not 'spiritual Israel' and does not replace national Israel, whose calling is irrevocable (Romans 11:28-29).
The Abrahamic, Davidic and new covenants are unconditional and include national, territorial promises to ethnic Israel that will be fulfilled literally (Genesis 15; 2 Samuel 7; Jeremiah 31:35-37).
History is structured by dispensations; Scofield counted seven (innocence, conscience, human government, promise, law, grace, kingdom), though the number is not essential.
The church began at Pentecost (Acts 2; 1 Corinthians 12:13) and is a 'mystery' not revealed in the Old Testament (Ephesians 3:3-6; Colossians 1:26).
Salvation in every dispensation is by grace through faith; dispensations differ in revelation and stewardship, not in the way of salvation.
God's ultimate purpose is his own glory, manifested through Israel, the church and the nations, not through the church alone (doxological unity).
Eschatology follows: a future seventieth week of Daniel, a national conversion and restoration of Israel, and a literal millennial reign of Christ from Jerusalem.

history.text: Proponents note that the idea of distinct eras or 'economies' appears in Irenaeus, Augustine and later Protestants (Pierre Poiret, John Edwards, Isaac Watts), and that Puritans and others expected a restoration of the Jews; however the system as such is modern.

John Nelson Darby, a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, systematised the sharp Israel-church distinction, the church as a heavenly people, the postponement of the kingdom, and the pretribulational rapture, and spread the view through extensive travels in Britain and North America.

The Scofield Reference Bible (1909, 1917) made dispensationalism the dominant framework of American fundamentalism; Lewis Sperry Chafer founded Dallas Theological Seminary (1924). Bible institutes (Moody, Biola) and prophecy conferences propagated it.

Charles Ryrie's Dispensationalism Today (1965; revised as Dispensationalism, 1995), John Walvoord and J. Dwight Pentecost refined the system, abandoning the eternal heavenly/earthly dualism and responding to critics on salvation in the Old Testament.

From 1986 Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy argued for an inaugurated Davidic kingdom and a more unified view of God's plan while retaining a future for national Israel. Revised dispensationalism continues (Thomas Ice, Robert Thomas, The Master's Seminary), and Michael Vlach has articulated a non-supersessionist 'new creation' vision of Israel's future.

strengths: Upholds the irrevocability of God's specific promises to Abraham's physical descendants (Romans 11:29), guarding against supersessionism and its historical abuses.
Applies one hermeneutic consistently, seeking authorial intent in the original context before New Testament application.
Takes seriously the New Testament's continued distinction between Israel and the Gentiles even after Pentecost (Acts 3:19-21; Romans 11; 1 Corinthians 10:32).
Has been a powerful engine of Bible study, Bible institutes, missions and evangelism in modern evangelicalism.
Its progressive form shows a capacity for self-correction and fruitful dialogue with covenant theologians.

critiques.critique: The system is novel, unknown before the 1830s.
critiques.response: Dispensationalists answer that Scripture, not tradition, is the test; that elements (premillennialism, distinct economies, a future for Israel) are old; and that the doctrine of the church itself has developed through history. The real question is exegetical.

critiques.critique: The New Testament applies Israel's promises and titles directly to the church (Galatians 3:29; 6:16; 1 Peter 2:9; Hebrews 8), showing fulfilment rather than two programmes.
critiques.response: Dispensationalists argue that Gentile believers participate in Israel's spiritual blessings without becoming Israel (Ephesians 2:12-13; 3:6), and that typological application does not cancel the original national referents. Progressive dispensationalists speak of 'already' fulfilment in the church and 'not yet' fulfilment for national Israel.

critiques.critique: Calling the church a 'parenthesis' or 'mystery' unknown to the prophets marginalises the church and contradicts texts where the prophets foresaw Gentile inclusion (Amos 9:11-12 in Acts 15).
critiques.response: Revised and progressive dispensationalists clarify that the Gentiles' salvation was foreseen; the 'mystery' is their equal membership in one body with Jews (Ephesians 3:6). Progressive dispensationalists have largely dropped 'parenthesis' language.

critiques.critique: Strict literalism is applied selectively, and it implies a restored temple with sacrifices (Ezekiel 40-48), which seems to contradict Hebrews.
critiques.response: Dispensationalists hold that literal interpretation allows figures of speech while insisting on concrete referents. Those who expect millennial sacrifices interpret them as memorial or as providing ceremonial (not atoning) purification for mortal worshippers, not a return to Mosaic atonement; some dispensationalists read Ezekiel's temple less literally.

subViews.name: Classic dispensationalism
subViews.summary: Darby, Scofield, Chafer: two peoples with two eternal destinies (a heavenly church, an earthly Israel), the church age as a parenthesis, and the kingdom offered and postponed at Israel's rejection of Jesus.

subViews.name: Revised (normative) dispensationalism
subViews.summary: Ryrie, Walvoord, Pentecost, Ice: one people of God in the eternal state but distinct programmes in history; Ryrie's three essentials; strong emphasis on pretribulationism and a future Davidic kingdom not yet inaugurated.

subViews.name: Progressive dispensationalism
subViews.summary: Blaising, Bock, Saucy: the dispensations are progressive stages of one unfolding kingdom; Christ's Davidic reign was inaugurated at the ascension; the church is a phase of the kingdom, not a parenthesis; national Israel still has a distinct future. Critics on both sides have called it a halfway house; proponents call it a maturing of the tradition.

subViews.name: Ultra- / hyper-dispensationalism
subViews.summary: A minority view (E. W. Bullinger, the 'Acts 28' and 'mid-Acts' positions) that places the beginning of the body-of-Christ church later than Pentecost, often limiting water baptism or the Lord's Supper. Mainstream dispensationalists (e.g. Ryrie) have rejected it.

name: Progressive Covenantalism
tagline: The covenants unfold progressively and all converge on Christ and the new covenant.
selfDescription: Proponents describe their view as “kingdom through covenant”: a via media between dispensationalism and covenant theology that lets the biblical covenants, read in their progressive unfolding along the Bible's storyline, set the categories. 'Progressive' signals that revelation advances through the covenants; 'covenantalism' that the covenants are the backbone of Scripture. They speak of Christ as the antitype and 'true Israel' and of the church as the new covenant community, neither 'replacing' Israel nor running parallel to it.
summary: Progressive covenantalism, articulated chiefly by Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum in Kingdom through Covenant (2012), holds that God's kingdom comes through a series of covenants (creation/Adam, Noah, Abraham, Israel/Moses, David) which progressively reveal and are all fulfilled in Christ and the new covenant. Typology escalates: Israel, the land, the temple and the king are types fulfilled in Christ, so the land promise widens to the new creation. The church is the new covenant people of God in Christ, an entirely regenerate community (hence believer's baptism), neither a parenthesis beside Israel nor simply the continuation of a mixed covenant community. Most proponents are amillennial, some historic premillennial.
coreBeliefs: The biblical covenants form the backbone of Scripture's storyline, and must be read in their progressive unfolding: textual, epochal and canonical horizons.
There is a creation covenant with Adam as head of humanity (Genesis 1-2; Hosea 6:7), not usually framed as the classic 'covenant of works' and 'covenant of grace' schema.
Each covenant builds on the previous and all reach their fulfilment in Christ, who is the true Adam, true Israel, true seed of Abraham and true Davidic king.

Typology is escalating: types (Israel, land, temple, priesthood, sacrifices) are prophetic patterns fulfilled and surpassed in Christ, so the land promise expands to the whole new creation (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16).

Israel and the church: the church is not a replacement for Israel nor a separate people alongside it; it is the new covenant people in union with Christ, the true Israel, comprising believing Jews and Gentiles.
The new covenant community is entirely regenerate, all knowing the Lord and having the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:10-12), so baptism is for believers.

The Mosaic law as a covenant is fulfilled and ended in Christ; believers are under the 'law of Christ' (1 Corinthians 9:21; Galatians 6:2), with the moral will of God re-expressed in the new covenant.
Some proponents (e.g. Thomas Schreiner) affirm a future mass conversion of ethnic Jews in Romans 11:26, while denying a future national-territorial programme distinct from the church.

history.text: Progressive covenantalists draw on Reformed biblical theology (Geerhardus Vos), on Baptist covenant thought, and on 'New Covenant Theology' associated with John Reisinger, Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel (late 20th century), which stressed the discontinuity of the Mosaic covenant.

Old Testament scholar Peter Gentry and systematic theologian Stephen Wellum of Southern Baptist Theological Seminary published Kingdom through Covenant: A Biblical-Theological Understanding of the Covenants (2012; 2nd ed. 2018), coining 'progressive covenantalism' as a 'third way' between dispensationalism and covenant theology.

Wellum and Brent Parker edited Progressive Covenantalism: Charting a Course between Dispensational and Covenantal Theologies (2016), with essays on Israel, the land, the law and baptism. Thomas Schreiner's Covenant and God's Purpose for the World (2017) and related works broadened the approach, which is now influential among Baptist and broadly evangelical scholars.

Dispensationalists (e.g. Michael Vlach and seminary reviewers) welcome its covenant storyline but argue it undervalues ethnic Israel's future; covenant theologians welcome its unity of the people of God but reject its denial of a single covenant of grace and of infant baptism.

strengths: Builds its framework inductively from the biblical covenants themselves, read in canonical order, rather than from theological constructs.
Explains both continuity (one storyline, one people in Christ) and discontinuity (the newness of the new covenant).
Gives a Christ-centred account of Israel's promises that avoids both 'two peoples' and 'replacement' categories.
Grounds believer's baptism and a regenerate church membership in the nature of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:34).
Offers a bridge for dialogue between Reformed and dispensational traditions.

critiques.critique: Covenant theologians object that denying an overarching covenant of grace breaks the unity of salvation in both Testaments, and that a wholly regenerate new covenant community is unrealistic given apostasy warnings (Hebrews 6:4-8; 10:29).
critiques.response: Progressive covenantalists affirm one plan of salvation through Christ in every age but locate it in God's promise rather than a single covenant. Warning passages are means God uses to preserve true believers and expose false professors, not evidence of unregenerate covenant members.

critiques.critique: Dispensationalists argue that its typology functionally erases ethnic Israel's future and the land promises, amounting to a softer supersessionism.
critiques.response: Proponents reply that fulfilment in Christ is not erasure but escalation: Israel's promises are received in Christ by believing Jews and Gentiles, the land expands into the new creation, and many still affirm a future turning of Jews to Christ (Romans 11:26).

critiques.critique: It is too new and too close to New Covenant Theology, raising concerns about antinomianism and the abiding role of the moral law.
critiques.response: Gentry and Wellum distinguish their approach from some forms of New Covenant Theology and affirm that God's moral will is binding on believers; they argue that it is mediated through Christ's law, which includes and fulfils the moral content of the Old Testament.

subViews.name: Kingdom through Covenant (Gentry–Wellum)
subViews.summary: The defining articulation: a creation covenant with Adam, the covenants as the Bible's backbone, escalating typology, Christ as the true Israel, a regenerate new covenant community, and the land fulfilled in the new creation.

subViews.name: New Covenant Theology
subViews.summary: A closely related earlier movement (John Reisinger, Tom Wells, Fred Zaspel) that stresses the discontinuity of the Mosaic covenant and the primacy of the law of Christ. Progressive covenantalists share much with it but present a more developed covenantal biblical theology.

subViews.name: Israel and Romans 11 in progressive covenantalism
subViews.summary: Proponents agree that Christ is the true Israel and that no separate national-territorial programme remains, but differ on Romans 11:26: some (e.g. Schreiner) expect a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews into the church; others read 'all Israel' as the elect of Israel or the whole people of God.
